Why Permethrin, Not Repellent

There's an important difference between permethrin and topical repellents like DEET or picaridin. Repellents make you smell bad to bugs — they wear off, wash off, and need reapplication. Permethrin is a contact insecticide that bonds to fabric fibers at a molecular level. When a tick or mosquito lands on your treated clothing, it absorbs a lethal dose and dies within seconds. You don't smell it, you don't feel it, and it keeps working through multiple wash cycles.

A landmark University of Rhode Island study found that treating shoes and socks with permethrin reduced the likelihood of a tick bite by 73.6 times compared to untreated clothing. That's not a marginal improvement — it's a complete change in risk profile.

Pro tip: Permethrin is for clothing and gear only — never apply it directly to skin. Pair treated clothes with a picaridin-based topical repellent on exposed skin for full coverage. Sawyer makes both, and they work together perfectly.

Real-World Coverage Test

Permethrin isn't cheap per ounce, so you want to know your bottle goes as far as possible. We tested both sprays on identical sets of outdoor clothing: one long-sleeve shirt, one pair of hiking pants, one pair of socks, and one backpack.

The EPA recommends roughly 4.5 ounces of permethrin solution per full outfit (shirt + pants + socks). With a 24 oz bottle, that means you can treat about 5 full outfits with either product.

However, the Sawyer trigger spray delivers a more consistent fan pattern than Ben's. We found Sawyer's spray covered fabric more evenly with less overspray, meaning less product wasted into the air. Your results may vary slightly depending on technique, but in controlled testing, Sawyer covered more surface area per spray.

Durability: Does 6 Weeks Hold Up?

Both products claim protection through 6 washes or 6 weeks of wear, whichever comes first. In practice, we found permethrin retention depends more on how you wash your gear than which product you use:

  • Wash treated items in cold water
  • Use mild detergent (no bleach or fabric softener)
  • Air dry in sunlight (UV exposure breaks down permethrin faster than washing)
  • Store treated clothing away from direct light

Follow those rules, and both Sawyer and Ben's will comfortably hit the 6-week mark. Skimp on care, and both will degrade faster — making the higher price of Ben's an even harder pill to swallow.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use Sawyer permethrin on my dog's gear?

Yes — permethrin-treated dog beds, collars, and bandanas are common. Just don't apply it directly to your pet's skin. There are permethrin-based spot-on treatments made specifically for dogs.

Is permethrin safe for tents and backpacks?

Yes, it won't damage nylon, polyester, or coated fabrics. Apply to mesh tent walls for extra protection, but avoid getting spray on sleeping bag insulation or down fill.

How often should I retreat?

Every 6 weeks or 6 washes, whichever comes first. Mark your calendar — it's easy to forget, and ticks don't take weekends off.

Does permethrin work on all insects?

Sawyer's formula kills mosquitoes, ticks, chiggers, mites, and over 55 species of insects. It's not effective against wasps, bees, or spiders — those need targeted treatments.
